seo.title: LuxBox — Product design case study | Max Zlydar
seo.description: End-to-end product design of LuxBox, a mystery-box platform with real luxury prizes: research, trust-first UX, retention mechanics and a design system.
seo.keywords: LuxBox, mystery box, iGaming, e-commerce, product design, UX research, UI, design system, case study, Max Zlydar
seo.ogTitle: LuxBox — Product design case study | Max Zlydar

intro.title: LuxBox is a mystery-box platform where people win real luxury items — watches, gold, sneakers. I designed it end-to-end around the one problem the whole category has: trust.

role.label: My role
role.value: Lead Product Designer — research, UX, UI, design system, brand

cover.challengeText: Launch a mystery-box platform that feels as exciting as a casino but as trustworthy as a store — for casual players and resellers alike, on web and mobile.

context.title: The product earns on every box opened
context.body: The margin is built into each box's prize pool, so the growth model is simple: turn a visitor into someone who opens their first box, then give them a reason to open the next one. Every design decision was measured against two numbers — first-open conversion and boxes per user.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: Mystery boxes have a reputation: hidden odds, rigged drops, prizes that never arrive. Users come in curious and leave suspicious. If the interface doesn't prove fairness on every screen, nobody risks their first €10.

research.label: What users told us
research.source: Survey of 120 target users + 12 in-depth interviews

method.title: The problem wasn't excitement. It was proof.
method.body: I started with a briefing and secondary research of 6 competing platforms, then moved to interviews and a survey. Competitors had plenty of hype — confetti, sounds, flashing prizes. What none of them had was a convincing answer to «can I trust this?». That became the design brief.

insight.label: Key insight
insight.headline: Half the audience plays for the thrill. The other half plays for ROI.
insight.speedLine: One interface had to give Alexa emotion and Jordan evidence — at the same time.

prioritization.title: Not every feature deserves a sprint
prioritization.body: With a team of five, I ran a Kano analysis of the candidate features and mapped them on value vs. effort. Box classes turned out to be a basic need — without them nothing else matters. Odds display and live drops were delighters. Sound on opening was a reverse feature: it irritates active users, so it became optional.

kano.r1Why: Sets clear expectations and fair conditions for everyone
kano.r2Why: The faster and more precise, the more satisfied users are
kano.r3Why: Turns fine print into a reason to trust the product
kano.r4Why: Social proof that real people win real prizes
kano.r6Why: No impact on efficiency or experience — deprioritized
kano.chartTitle: Kano model: how each type of feature affects user satisfaction

odds.label: 01 · Clear odds
odds.title: Odds you can read in two seconds
odds.body: Every box shows its full prize list with drop rates, plus a «Provably fair» link right next to the Open button. Odds stopped being fine print and became part of the product: the higher the price, the better the chance — and users can see it.

live.label: 02 · Live drops
live.title: Social proof beats any «100% fair» badge
live.body: A live feed of real openings runs across the top of the home page. Seeing that someone just won a Rolex does more for trust than any promise in the footer — and it pulls new visitors straight into the featured boxes.

classes.label: 03 · Simplified UI
classes.title: Value you understand without reading
classes.body: Boxes are split into 10 color-coded classes, from €2 to €40,000. Color tells you the price tier before you read a single number: Alexa scans, Jordan filters.

architecture.title: One navigation for novices and pros
architecture.body: Six top-level sections and a shallow two-level hierarchy. A new user reaches their first box in 2 taps; a power user gets to battles and the wallet without digging through menus.

retention.label: Retention
retention.title: The first box is acquisition. The second one is the business.
retention.body: Trust brings users in; mechanics bring them back. I designed three loops, each tied to a need from the interviews:
retention.item1: Battles — users open the same boxes head-to-head, the winner takes everything. Pure emotion for Alexa.
retention.item2: Leaderboard — monthly prizes for the top players keep the competitive core active.
retention.item3: Ranks — seven levels from Starter to Diamond that grow with activity. Recognition and status — exactly what Jordan asked for.

gamification.label: Gamification
gamification.title: Progress you can see is progress you want to continue
gamification.body: To grow engagement, we added a gamification layer: ranks and a monthly leaderboard. For a product designer this isn't decoration — it's a way to turn single visits into a habit:
gamification.item1: Visible progress. People are more motivated the closer they see themselves to the next level (goal-gradient effect). A rank bar gives every opening a meaning beyond the prize itself.
gamification.item2: Status and comparison. A leaderboard and rank badges let users see where they stand among others — a strong driver for a competitive, collector-type audience.
gamification.item3: A reason to come back. Monthly resets and new ranks create regular return triggers, which directly supports retention and the number of boxes per user.

mobile.title: Mobile is where most boxes are opened
mobile.body: Most of the audience plays from a phone, so mobile got its own layout rather than a squeezed desktop: a box can be opened one-handed and the result lands in the thumb zone.

compliance.label: Compliance
compliance.title: Regulation is part of the interface
compliance.body: Gambling products work under different laws in every country, so in some cases the interface had to adapt to legal requirements. Instead of a generic error, a user from a restricted region gets a clear, on-brand screen: what happened, that we're working on it, and how to stay in touch — a dead end turned into a future comeback.

system.title: A brand that stands out in a flashy market
system.body: Competitors shout with neon and casino gold. LuxBox speaks calmly: monospace type, a 12-column grid, soft gradient noise and a strict palette — it looks like a premium store, not a slot machine. ~60 components cut design-to-dev handoff time roughly in half.

marketing.title: Design didn't stop at the product
marketing.body: Together with our marketer I built a template system for launch campaigns and social media, so the brand stayed consistent from the first ad to the box opening screen.

testing.label: Usability testing
testing.title: Two rounds with 8 users before launch
testing.body: Key task: «Find the chance to win the top prize in this box». After round one I moved the odds next to the Open button and added sorting by drop rate.

results.title: Results
results.stat3Label: Boxes opened per user per month
results.details: LuxBox launched on web and mobile with a single design system and a trust-first UX. Transparent odds and live drops removed the category's biggest objection, while battles and ranks gave users a reason to come back.

seo.title: Space Planning — Product design case study | Max Zlydar
seo.description: Product design of Space Planning, a B2B SaaS for grocery retail: a guided planogram editor, in-place validation and financial reports for staff without planning experience.
seo.keywords: Space Planning, planogram, retail, B2B SaaS, product design, UX research, dashboard, design system, case study, Max Zlydar
seo.ogTitle: Space Planning — Product design case study | Max Zlydar

intro.title: Space Planning is a B2B SaaS for grocery retail that turns shelf layout from guesswork into data. I designed the platform end-to-end so office staff with no planning background can build planograms that actually sell.

cover.challengeText: Turn a scattered MVP into a planogram platform that untrained store staff can use from day one — and connect every shelf decision to sales, stock and supply data.

quote.label: Voice of the client
quote.text: «The planogram is supposed to be implemented on the shelf. But it doesn't work. It provides too few facings for the fast-moving store brand article, but too many facings for products that do not perform. Some products are in the planogram even though they are not profitable for the store and are marked down again and again.»
quote.name: Thomas J.

context.title: A shelf is the most expensive square meter in a store
context.body: Every planogram decides which products get space and how much. Too few facings for fast movers means empty shelves and lost sales; too many for slow movers means stock that gets marked down again and again. The platform had one job — make every shelf meter earn — so I measured design decisions against sales per shelf meter and inventory on hand.

market.label: The market problem
market.f1Label: of sales are lost to out-of-stocks in traditional retail
market.f2Label: of shelf space goes unused with traditional planning
market.f3Label: months of delay between sales strategy and in-store execution
market.body: This gap between strategy and the real shelf is exactly where the product earns money — and where the interface has to be fast and foolproof enough for people who are not planners.

problem.title: Problem
problem.body: Merchandise placement was handled by office staff with no planning or analytics experience. Existing tools assumed expertise they didn't have, so layouts were built on gut feeling:
problem.item1: Inefficient space — overloaded zones and shelves limit product accessibility.
problem.item2: Disorganized categories — frequently bought items are spread out, slowing down shopping.
problem.item3: Poor placement — high-margin and popular items end up in weak positions.
problem.item4: No room for change — new arrivals and edits break the layout every time.

process.label: Process
process.title: Two years: from the first interview to a mature product
process.body: I didn't hand over mockups and leave. For two years I owned the product experience: designed the MVP, adapted it to real client stores after launch, shipped new features and kept simplifying what already existed — every step backed by usability tests, analytics and client feedback.
process.chartTitle: Product roadmap 2024–2025: discovery, MVP design, testing, launch, new features, optimization and ongoing support
process.s2: MVP design: user flow, prototypes, design system
process.s5: New features: financial reports, version compare, Quick Tips, shelf parameters
process.k1Label: of continuous product work, not a one-off handoff
process.k2Label: screens and flows designed and maintained
process.k3Label: validated with usability tests and client feedback

insight.label: Key insight
insight.headline: Users don't read instructions — they try things.
insight.speedLine: So the interface had to guide and check the user by itself, instead of relying on training.

flow.title: Mapping the work before drawing screens
flow.body: 35+ screens started as one user flow: access requests, categories, planograms, exports, reports and logs. Mapping it first let the team agree on scope and dependencies before a single pixel was drawn — and later made every new feature land in the right place.

solution.label: Solution
solution.title: Move the expertise into the interface
solution.body: Instead of teaching staff to become planners, I built three things into the product: a visual editor, validation in place of training, and guidance at the moment of action.

editor.label: 01 · Visual editor
editor.title: See the shelf, not a spreadsheet
editor.body: Planograms are edited on a visual shelf: drag products, change facings, open any item to set its size, value and tags. Staff work with what they see in the store, not with product codes.
editor.why: Staff think in shelves and products, not in tables and codes. A visual editor removes the translation step where most mistakes happen.
editor.effect: First store-level planograms in under 2 weeks instead of 20+ for a Fortune 500 grocer.

validation.label: 02 · Validation
validation.title: Mistakes are caught on the screen, not in the store
validation.body: Every change is checked against the real shelf. Overflowing sections and height mismatches are highlighted in place with a plain-language hint, so errors that used to surface after installation are fixed before export.
validation.why: An error found after installation costs a store visit and lost sales. An error found on screen costs one click.
validation.effect: Shelf space utilisation grew from 90% to 96%, with higher shelf compliance in stores.

tips.label: 03 · Guidance
tips.title: Onboarding inside the work, not before it
tips.body: First-time users get short Quick Tips right where they act: select a store, open a mudmap, rebuild the planogram. No manual to read, no training session to book.
tips.why: Training sessions don't scale to thousands of stores. Guidance at the moment of action does.
tips.effect: Planning effort went down — teams were redeployed to vendor and strategy work.

analytics.label: Analytics
analytics.title: Every layout change shows its money effect
analytics.body: Financial reports connect planograms to sales, profit, stock and displaced products. Category managers see planned vs actual results and which SKUs lost space — and act on data instead of intuition.
analytics.why: Category managers have to defend every layout change to the business. Numbers next to the shelf make that conversation short.
analytics.effect: +17% profit uplift vs. control stores for a global health & beauty retailer.

compare.title: Compare versions before rolling out
compare.body: Any planogram version can be compared with the previous one by sales, units, products and days of supply, with a one-click reset for a single value. Decisions became reversible — so teams experimented more.
compare.why: When a change can be undone, people stop being afraid to try. Fear of mistakes was the main brake on optimization.
compare.effect: Unlimited planogram scenarios, with changes made in minutes instead of days.

params.title: Precision where it matters
params.body: For the physical setup, pegboards and shelves keep exact parameters — offsets, peg spacing, class and type — so what's planned is exactly what gets installed.

details.label: Interface details
details.title: The details that make a complex tool feel simple
details.body: A planning tool is used for hours every day, so small decisions add up. Each pattern below solves a concrete friction point found in testing or support tickets.
details.itemText: ID, segment, block and priority without leaving the shelf. A «Saved» mark removes the fear of losing changes.
details.tipText: A 6-step tour that points at the real controls — store selector, MudMap, POG, reports. Experienced users skip it, new ones don't get lost.
details.filterText: Category → subcategory in one panel. Counters show the result before you click, so there are no empty searches.
details.errorsText: Problems are grouped by type (low width, item too tall) with SKUs listed. Users fix a class of errors at once, not one by one.
details.inlineText: Change height or width right in the tooltip and confirm with one tap. No modal, no context switch.
details.searchText: Lists with hundreds of items get a search field and match highlighting. Choosing takes seconds, not scrolling.
details.tagsText: Up to 4 tags per product with fixed colors. The limit keeps the shelf readable, colors make sorting visual.
details.tableText: Ranged / Unranged status is visible in every row; a page number field lets users jump through long reports instead of clicking «next» 20 times.
details.progressText: Long operations show progress and a shortcut to open all results — users always know the system is working.
details.uploadText: Product master files are imported by dropping a CSV. Clear empty, loaded and error states remove the most common onboarding blocker — getting data in.
details.hint: Every card below is interactive — click, type and save. Your changes stay in this browser.
details.itemTry: Try it: click any product on the shelf.
details.tipTry: Try it: press Next to walk through the tour, or Skip.
details.inlineTry: Try it: change width or height, then save with ✓ or cancel with ✕.
details.filterTry: Try it: pick a category and tick subcategories — the button counts products.
details.errorsTry: Try it: click an SKU to mark it fixed, open «Show more».
details.tagsTry: Try it: remove a tag with × or add one with +. A fifth tag isn't allowed.
details.tableTry: Try it: type a page number or use the arrows.
details.uploadTry: Try it: drop any file here — a .csv is accepted, other formats show the error state. Nothing is uploaded.

system.title: A design system that scales with the catalog
system.body: A component library with every state — default, hover, active, disabled, error — so developers never guessed and the product stayed consistent across 35+ screens for two years. New departments and products are added in seconds by office staff, without a designer.

site.title: Designing how the product sells
site.body: A B2B product is bought by people who never open it: directors and procurement. I designed the website as a sales funnel that answers their questions in the order they ask them — what is it, does it work, what can it do, how much, how do I start.
site.label: Marketing website
site.heroTitle: One sentence of value, one action
site.heroBody: The hero says what the product does in plain words and offers a single action — «Request a demo». A real dashboard below proves this is a working product, not a concept.
site.proofBody: B2B buyers need numbers to sell the purchase internally. Results (+4% sales, −6% inventory, +15% efficiency) come right after the hero, before any feature list.
site.featuresBody: Five capabilities — replenishment, assortment, demand, planogram and floor planning — named the way retail teams describe their work, with the product shown next to them.
site.pricingBody: Two clear tiers. Enterprise is marked as recommended to anchor the choice, and a first-year discount on Standard lowers the risk of the first purchase.
site.ctaBody: An accordion closes the main objections — integration with existing systems, store-level uniqueness, results. The final CTA lets a prospect upload a CSV and see suggestions on their own data before any sales call.

testing.label: Usability testing
testing.title: Usability tests after every major release
testing.body: Each big release went through moderated tests with category managers. Example from one round — key task: «Add a new product to the planogram and fix all placement errors». After round one I added in-place error hints and Quick Tips for the first steps.

clients.label: The product in production
clients.title: Used by global retailers every week
clients.body: The platform I designed runs real category management for convenience, grocery and health & beauty chains.
clients.c1Label: store-level planograms created weekly across 3,000+ stores
clients.c2Label: to first store-level plans instead of 20+ weeks, in 100+ stores
clients.quoteText: «[The platform] successfully managed our network-wide store-level assortment roll-out during a time when shopper behaviour changed more in 6 months than in 35 years.»

results.title: Results
results.details: Space Planning turned shelf planning from a specialist task into an everyday routine for store office staff. Guided editing, in-place validation and financial reports let non-planners make data-driven decisions — and let the business scale store-level planning without growing the planning team.
results.stat5Label: To first store-level plans, down from 20+
results.source: Results of retail clients using the platform, as published by the product company.

seo.title: Levels & subscriptions UX — Case study | Max Zlydar
seo.description: Reworking levels and subscription UX for clearer progression and stronger conversion to paid plans—research-led product design case study by Max Zlydar.
seo.keywords: subscriptions, levels, conversion, UX, product design, growth, case study, Max Zlydar
seo.ogTitle: Levels & subscriptions UX — Case study | Max Zlydar

intro.title: Blum levels redesign that improved subscription conversion.

team.myRoleDesc: Product designer responsible for levels UX/UI

role.label: Challenge:
role.value: Users didn’t understand how levels worked, why they mattered, or how they affected the subscription — and conversion suffered.

cover.dataTitle: What we saw in the data
cover.dataText: A large share of users dropped off one or two steps before subscribing. Interviews showed people didn’t understand what levels gave them or how far they had progressed.
cover.hypothesisText: If we make the level system transparent and tie it to concrete value (bonuses, limits, perks), users can decide on a subscription more easily.

changes.title: What we changed
changes.desc1: Simpler progress logic, a clear visual level path, and plain descriptions of what unlocks at each stage.
changes.desc2: We emphasized actions that move users forward: completing tasks, trading, and engaging with the product.

next.title: What’s next
next.body: The full case covers hypotheses, level maps, A/B tests, and impact on key metrics. Reach out if you’d like a detailed walkthrough.

intro.title: Research template design for Yandex Vzglyad

cover.contextText: The business wanted to launch research faster and spend less analyst time explaining “what exactly we need.”
cover.productText: We mapped typical business tasks and turned them into ready-made research scenarios with a clear structure, questions, and expected outcomes.

how.title: How it works
how.body: The client picks a task (e.g. creative testing or concept validation), gets a template with questions and structure, and sees what output they’ll receive.

business.title: Business value
business.body: Businesses get a fast start on research without extra calls and emails, while the team can focus on complex requests instead of repetitive ones.
